text: Welcome to session seven, the first session on network models.
In one hour, we plan the installation of CellCo's storage system as a project network and find its critical path.
Here is the plan.
First, activity-on-node networks and the forward and backward passes. Then your group builds the network from cards. We finish with slack and the critical path.
CellCo will install a ten megawatt hour storage system at its plant. The project has eight activities.
It starts with the site survey and permits. Then come the detailed design, the procurement of battery containers and of the power conversion system, and the civil works.
Installation and commissioning follow. The table lists each activity's predecessors and its most likely duration in weeks.
In an activity-on-node network, each box is an activity, and each arrow says that one activity must finish before the next can start.
For example, installing the containers needs both the containers and the foundations, so F has two arrows coming in, from C and from D.
The boxes and arrows in amber lie on a critical path. We will see how to find it on the next slide.
The forward pass finds the earliest times. An activity can start when its last predecessor finishes, so its earliest start is the largest earliest finish of its predecessors.
The backward pass starts from the project end and finds the latest times. An activity must finish before its first successor has to start.
Total slack is the latest start minus the earliest start. Activities with zero slack are critical: any delay to them delays the whole project.
Here, every activity except D has zero slack. D, the civil works, has six weeks of slack.
Activity. Work in groups of four for twenty minutes.
Your group receives the eight activity cards in random order. Build the network on the sheet, with every arrow pointing from a predecessor to its successor.
Then write the earliest and latest times on each card, and find the project duration and the critical activities.
Finish with a gallery walk: check another group's network, and correct one error if you find one.
The project takes nineteen weeks.
There are two critical paths, both nineteen weeks long: A, B, C, F, H, and A, B, E, G, H.
Only the civil works have slack. They can start up to six weeks late without delaying the project.
Two critical paths make the plan fragile. A delay to either the containers or the power conversion system delays commissioning, and shortening only one of them gains nothing.
Choose an activity and change its duration. The network recomputes the earliest and latest times and highlights the critical activities.
Try shortening the containers, activity C, from eight weeks to six. The project still takes nineteen weeks, because the other critical path does not change.
Then try lengthening the civil works beyond their slack, and watch them become critical.
Let us summarize.
An activity-on-node network shows the order of the work. The forward pass gives the earliest times, and the backward pass the latest.
CellCo's installation takes nineteen weeks, with two critical paths. Only the civil works have slack.
With parallel critical paths, shortening one activity alone does not shorten the project.
After lunch, in session eight, we add uncertain durations, estimate the chance of finishing on time, and decide what to pay to finish earlier.
For the exit ticket: the civil works team asks to start four weeks late. Can the plant manager agree without delaying commissioning? Write down the number that decides it.
